title: Superconducting Chip Claims: Don't Change Process Node, Change Temperature Zone—28nm Logic Could Hit 5nm Performance
dek: Move logic to liquid-helium temperatures and replace transistors with superconducting switches. That's Snowcap's bet: first tape out a RISC-V chip, then claim 28nm-class logic can deliver 5nm-class performance.
why: If you're watching the compute power wall, this episode lays out a third path—not shrinking transistors, but moving the entire logic to liquid-helium temperatures; a former Intel CEO has placed his bet. The risks and numbers are all on the table, worth a listen.
who: Hard-tech investors who want to verify whether superconducting computing is a real path or just a story, and CPU/supercomputer architects studying the chip power wall.
skip: If you're familiar with overclocking and liquid nitrogen cooling, you can skip the overclocking preamble from 0:00 to 2:01.

points.h: The ceiling for extreme overclocking is cooling, not the chip
points.body: The episode opens with the overclocking industry: everyday chips use air cooling, higher-power ones use water cooling, and beyond that you need dry ice, liquid nitrogen, and other sub-zero media. Extreme overclockers push voltage to chase maximum frequencies, making chips hotter and hotter, so they have to cool them in increasingly extreme ways. The host says he was once an extreme overclocker and took second place in the world—though it only lasted a day and a half. His key reference point: this kind of overclocking is only for running benchmark tests for a few minutes at 8.5GHz, whereas true superconducting computing isn't chasing instantaneous records but logic that runs at near-zero power.

points.h: The expensive part of liquid-helium overclocking isn't the helium, it's the transfer tube
points.body: Going from liquid nitrogen to liquid helium, physics starts to get in the way. Liquid helium costs about 20 times as much as liquid nitrogen (which runs about a dollar a liter), but that's not the main expense: the transfer tube that moves liquid helium from a large storage tank into a 3-4 kg copper overclocking pot costs $5,000 per use. Intel and Asus have both done liquid-helium overclocking, with records already past 9GHz. The host warns that material behavior changes dramatically at such temperatures—some platforms have a 'cold bug' where the system simply won't start when it gets too cold; only platforms without the cold bug are suitable for liquid-helium play.

points.h: The allure of superconductivity isn't speed, it's zero resistance
points.body: Overclocking is about squeezing frequency out of existing materials; superconductivity is a different narrative: electrons flow through superconducting materials with no resistance, which is like free transport. Currently, the vast majority of superconductors require extremely low temperatures, and room-temperature superconductivity remains in a state of repeated research claims and retractions. The key extrapolation here: if the entire chip's switching logic could operate in a superconducting state, the energy per operation would be 'several orders of magnitude' better than current laptops. The host deliberately makes a strong claim but then pulls back—superconductivity is still a holy grail, not yet in hand. This sets the stage for Snowcap's entry.

points.h: The former Intel CEO is betting on temperature zone, not process node
points.body: Snowcap Compute has just completed a seed round, and its board includes former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger. Their bet is on building superconducting chips that operate at roughly 4-15K, the liquid-helium temperature range. Structurally, it's no longer billions of transistors but a new type of switch that works at superconducting temperatures—the Josephson junction. For now, Snowcap's goal is to first build a RISC-V-class CPU at low temperatures, making power consumption nearly free; the cost is that the entire machine must be kept in the liquid-helium temperature range, and cooling itself consumes energy.

points.h: The new variable for superconducting logic is fitting into standard EDA flows
points.body: Long-term researchers are not scarce: US defense contractors have made chips integrating tens of millions of Josephson junctions, and IMEC has reached hundreds of millions, along with building supporting logic and EDA tools. Snowcap's differentiator is compatibility: they say this kind of superconducting logic can fit into standard EDA flows and can be taped out on ordinary CMOS processes, using niobium titanium nitride as the material. The core conclusion the host heard: the energy-efficiency advantage from superconductivity is equivalent to using 28nm logic to achieve performance close to a 5nm chip—note this isn't a smaller process node, but the equivalent benefit from lower power.

points.h: Cryo CMOS is just an intermediate state; the real hurdle is scale
points.body: Snowcap plans to deliver its first chip in 2026, followed by a deployable RISC-V design. The intermediate state can be seen in cryo CMOS: it operates in the liquid-nitrogen temperature range of about 72-77K, and although it isn't superconducting, the low temperature itself reduces power consumption. The real hurdle is crossing from cryo CMOS into superconductivity; the host's skepticism is 'can you scale up performance at high levels'—being able to run and being able to scale commercially are two different things.

points.h: Cold startup isn't rare; the hard part is keeping the whole machine in liquid helium
points.body: This section provides a real-world footnote on cold tape-outs: AMD's first Zen 1 A0 sample, which leaked when AMD was most cash-strapped, could only start at sub-zero temperatures on dry ice due to a design flaw, and was later fixed to run at room temperature. This shows that low temperatures in testing and startup aren't unusual; but keeping an entire processor in the liquid-helium temperature range involves infrastructure issues, including helium supply—liquid helium is also the lifeblood of MRI machines' superconducting magnets, and there was a helium shortage a few years back.

points.h: Snowcap isn't selling IP; it's selling a sealed integrated system
points.body: Snowcap positions itself not as an IP seller but as delivering complete systems. The host's judgment is that precisely because of the infrastructure barrier of the liquid-helium temperature range, the product form will be nearly a sealed integrated system, and the software stack will need to be rebuilt. A seed-stage company still has Series A/B/C rounds to get through; however, they've already brought in advisors and former employees from Apple, Nvidia, and Google. On this topic, it's worth staying skeptical and also worth following.
